title: Separate shared-directory writing from deletion
goal: Prove sticky-bit deletion restrictions with two existing locked guest identities.
challenge: Use the existing ll-service and nobody identities only for files in a unique shared practice directory. Demonstrate cross-user writing to a deliberately writable file but refusal to unlink it; demonstrate owner and directory-owner exceptions. Do not change accounts.

steps.command: w=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/local-sticky.XXXXXX") && cd "$w" && pwd && here() { case "$w" in "$HOME"/local-sticky.??????) ;; *) return 19;; esac; test "${w%/*}" = "$HOME" && test -d "$w" && test ! -L "$w" && test "$(realpath -e "$w")" = "$w" && test "$(stat -c %U:%a "$w")" = learner:700 && test "$(pwd -P)" = "$w"; }; fresh() { for f; do test ! -e "$f" && test ! -L "$f" || return 19; done; }; here
steps.explanation: Create a unique learner-owned guest workspace; stop on error and record its absolute path. Reopening boots the disk, not these shell variables. Never use the host terminal.
steps.expected: A new private directory; no pre-existing files are changed.

steps.command: here && s=$(mktemp -d /tmp/ll-sticky.XXXXXX) && chmod 1777 "$s" && sg() { case "$s" in /tmp/ll-sticky.??????) ;; *) return 19;; esac; test "${s%/*}" = /tmp && test -d "$s" && test ! -L "$s" && test "$(realpath -e "$s")" = "$s" && test "$(stat -c %U:%a "$s")" = learner:1777 || return 19; for n in a b; do if test -e "$s/$n" || test -L "$s/$n"; then test ! -L "$s/$n" && test -f "$s/$n" && test "$(stat -c %h "$s/$n")" = 1 && test "$(stat -c %s "$s/$n")" -le 1024 || return 19; fi; done; members=$(find -P "$s" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name a ! -name b -print) || return 19; test -z "$members"; }; here && sg && getent passwd ll-service nobody
steps.explanation: Existing locked/non-login identities are invoked by approved guest sudo, not authenticated with credentials. Retain this exact generated path. Refuse setup failure.
steps.expected: A unique directory owned by learner, mode 1777.

steps.command: here && sg && fresh "$s/a" "$s/b" && { sudo runuser -u ll-service -- sh -c 'printf "service\n" > "$1/a" && chmod 0666 "$1/a"' sh "$s" && sudo runuser -u nobody -- sh -c 'printf "nobody\n" > "$1/b"' sh "$s"; }
steps.explanation: Create files as the actual identities. The writable a file separates content permissions from directory deletion restrictions.
steps.expected: a owned ll-service, b owned nobody.

steps.command:
here && sg && { sudo runuser -u nobody -- sh -c 'printf "append
" | dd of="$1/a" oflag=append,nofollow conv=notrunc,nocreat status=none' sh "$s" && printf 'service
append
' | cmp - "$s/a" && test "$(stat -c %U:%a "$s/a")" = ll-service:666 && { sudo runuser -u nobody -- rm -f -- "$s/a"; unlink_rc=$?; test "$unlink_rc" -ne 0 && test -f "$s/a" && printf 'service
append
' | cmp - "$s/a" && test "$(stat -c %U "$s/b")" = nobody && stat -c '%U %a %n' "$s" "$s/a" "$s/b"; }; }
steps.explanation: Sticky restricts unlink/rename, not ordinary writes to an existing writable file. This guest also has protected_regular=2: shell >> uses O_CREAT and can be refused independently. The bounded GNU dd command opens only the known existing file: nocreat refuses a missing target, nofollow refuses a final symlink, notrunc preserves bytes, and append writes at the end. Do not change kernel policy. -f avoids an rm prompt; it cannot bypass sticky permission checks.
steps.expected: Append succeeds, cross-owner unlink fails and a remains.

steps.command: here && sg && { sudo runuser -u ll-service -- rm -f -- "$s/a" && rm -f -- "$s/b" && rmdir -- "$s"; }
steps.explanation: File owner may unlink a; learner, as directory owner, may unlink b. Root is also an exception, but using root alone would not test ordinary-user restrictions.
steps.expected: Both exact files and shared directory removed.

hints: Use actual identities and immediate status.
Compare file writing with directory entry removal.
Directory owner and file owner are exceptions.
review: I retained actual output and checked the required contents, metadata or identity, not just command success.
I can explain the stated limitations, demonstrate the incorrect case, preserve originals and clean up only my recorded workspace.
